title: Designing dashboards people can scan
metaTitle: Dashboard UX design people can scan
excerpt: Dashboard UX design is a hierarchy: what changed, what needs a decision, and what can wait. Equal-weight charts make people hunt for the job.
alt: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it. Building a scannable view starts in that editor, as a hierarchy rather than a wall of charts.
caption: The first glance should know where to land. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should appear first on a dashboard?
faqs.answer: Lead with what changed since the last meaningful visit, then with the items that need a decision. Totals and trend charts that nobody will act on today can follow, or live one step away. A number without a comparison is trivia. A comparison the job uses is the start of a scan.

faqs.question: How many charts belong on the first screen?
faqs.answer: Only the chart that answers the first minute better than a sentence or a list. Many dashboards are a report nobody opens, wrapped around the one list people use. Put that list first. Move extra series to the detail view, after someone has chosen an object.

faqs.question: What makes a row scannable?
faqs.answer: A name the person recognizes, a status that explains why the row is here, and one next step. Say how the list is sorted. Avoid truncating the only word that distinguishes two rows. A menu of seven equal actions on every row turns the scan back into reading.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Dashboard UX design is a hierarchy a person can scan: what changed, what needs a decision, and what can wait. A dashboard is not a poster of every number the system can compute. It is a view for a repeated job, arranged so the eye knows where to land before it knows every label.

If the first screen is twelve charts of equal size, there is no hierarchy. There is a wall. Walls look thorough in a design review. On a Tuesday morning they are slow, and Tuesday morning is when the view has to work. The person did not open it to admire the chart library. They opened it to see whether anything requires them.

## Three bands, in an order that stays put

**What changed.** Put the difference from the last visit, or from the period the job cares about, where the eye starts. A number without a comparison is a trivia card. "42 open" means more beside "6 more than yesterday," in the words the work already uses. Name the period. A figure from last quarter sitting quietly next to a figure from this morning is a false comparison, and people will make it if you do not label the time.

**What needs a decision.** Under the change, list the items a person can act on. Each row should carry the object, the reason it is on the list, and the action. If nothing needs a decision, say so. An empty decision list is a successful morning, not a broken widget. Treat it as a state you write on purpose.

**What can wait.** Trends, archives, and totals nobody will act on today go last, or one step away. They are allowed to exist. They are not allowed to shout at the same volume as the decision. A quiet section is a design choice. It means you know the difference between reference and work.

Trade Moai, a public Hanabi trading interface concept, is organized around scanning rather than around a grid of equal panels. Mentioning it is about that structure. It is not a claim about markets or results. A person should be able to see what moved and what might require a choice. You can judge any reference the same way: does the first glance answer the job, or does it ask you to start reading from the top left and hope?

## People will skip most of the words

Nielsen Norman Group reported in 2011 that visitors have time to read only about a quarter of the text on the web pages they actually open, and that people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds when the value is unclear. [The article](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) studied web pages. A dashboard is a page with the same limit. The person will sample. They will not read your captions in order. Hierarchy is how you choose which quarter they are likely to hit.

Labels on the first band have to be plain. "Needs review" beats a phrase invented for a pitch. Put the unit on the number. If a chart needs a paragraph before it means anything, it is in the wrong band, or it should have been a sentence. Sentences are allowed on a dashboard. They are often clearer than a sparkline nobody can decode at a glance.

Color is a signal. Use one color for "a person should look," one for "this is fine," and a neutral for the rest. A rainbow of series on the first screen forces the scan to start over. Extra series belong on the detail view, after someone has chosen to look. Decorative color on a chart is how a hierarchy gets flattened back into a poster.

## What belongs in a row

A scannable row has a name, a status, and a single next step. The name is the object as the person knows it in their work. The status is why the row is here. The next step is one control or one clear link. A menu of seven equally likely actions turns the row into a second product.

Truncate carefully. If the truncated part is the only word that distinguishes two rows, the scan has failed and the click has become mandatory. Give long names the width. Let secondary facts wrap, or move them to the detail. The row is a recognition test, not a storage format.

Sorting should match the job, and it should be visible. A decision list often sorts by urgency or by age. Alphabetical order is comfortable for the database and sometimes wrong for the morning. A list that reorders itself without a stated rule feels unreliable, and people stop trusting the top row. Say "oldest first" or "largest change" in the interface, not only in a tooltip nobody opens.

## Design the first minute, then stop

Ask what the person does in the first minute. Design that, and then stop adding. Add a chart only when it answers the minute better than a list or a sentence. Many overviews are a report nobody reads, wrapped around the one list people came for. Lead with the list. You can keep the report. It does not have to win the first screen.

Hanabi designs this kind of view as the product, not as a skin on an analytics export. The implementation can be ordinary. One query for what changed. One query for what is waiting. A page that renders those before it renders anything else. React and TypeScript are enough to keep the empty morning and the error honest. The difficult part is refusing the third chart in the review where it looks impressive.

Detail pages can be richer. Once someone chooses an object, you have earned history, related records, and the controls that would have cluttered the scan. The way back should be obvious. The list should still be there, with the same sort and the same filters, when they return. A scan that forgets its filters on every return wastes the hierarchy you just designed.

Filters belong in the same discipline. A filter that changes what "needs a decision" means should be visible and easy to clear. Hidden filters are a support problem dressed up as power. If only one filter is used every day, consider making that view the default and leaving the rest one click away.

## A ten-minute review

Squint at the screen, or stand where body text disappears. You should still be able to point at what changed and at the first decision. If you cannot, the weights are too even. Then read the top item aloud. If the sentence needs a legend, rewrite the label until the legend is unnecessary.

Check a quiet day. A new account, or a morning with nothing to do, should still explain the view. A grid of zeroed charts looks broken when it is merely empty. Write "Nothing needs a decision" and, if there is a way to create work, show that action. The empty overview is part of the design, not a gap in the data.

Once the first screen has a hierarchy, the risk moves to the rest of the product. Extra screens creep back in around a clear dashboard. Read [fewer screens, a clearer product](/blog/fewer-screens-clearer-product) when the overview is in good shape and the surrounding flow is still a hallway.

Trade Moai sits with the other public interfaces on [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). Look for a first glance that has a job. Leave the chart style behind.
